title: Commit or Abstain? System One Decision Models, LLMs, and Missing Legal Authority
abstract: Given the enormous number of claims to be checked, verifiable legal AI requires scalable, cost-effective models that answer the practical needs of law. System One decision models are built on large language models but, instead of generating text, return a calibrated probability for each option. This suits the verification of legal authority, where the question is closed: a given holding, or none of them. We test whether such models abstain when the correct authority is missing. We extend CaseHOLD with an abstention condition in which the correct holding is replaced in 1,670 of 5,314 items, and compare four decision models with six generative LLMs. When no option is correct, generative LLMs still pick one in 38-86% of items; the most cautious decision model does so in 30%. On standard CaseHOLD, a decision model matches the best generative LLM (88.1% vs. 88.2%) at 1/55 of the cost. Accepting that LLM's answer only when a decision model agrees halves its wrong citations, and distilling a decision model's probabilities into Qwen3-8B, without labels, yields a well-calibrated local model. Legal AI should be judged by its wrong citations, not by accuracy alone.

title: A KAN-based Non-linear Factorization for Embedding Layer Compression
abstract: Among existing embedding compression approaches, low-rank factorization provides a simple and mathematically principled solution by approximating the embedding matrix with a reduced-rank decomposition. However, its practical effectiveness is often limited, as the resulting linear bottleneck constrains representational capacity. To overcome these limitations, we propose an enhanced factorization scheme that increases expressive power by introducing learnable non-linear projections within the compressed embedding layer. Our method is inspired by the Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KAN) paradigm, which replaces fixed linear transformations with learnable univariate functions. Despite promising results in other domains, applications of KANs in NLP remain scarce and have so far been largely limited to final or task specific layers, rather than core representational components such as embedding layers. We evaluate the proposed approach by integrating the compressed embedding layer into the Skip-gram framework and comparing it against a standard low-rank baseline under matched parameter budgets on the Word Analogy and Semantic Similarity benchmarks. We further introduce an effective initialization strategy from a pre-trained, uncompressed embedding layer. The behavior of the model is analyzed both immediately after initialization and after a brief post-initialization refinement phase, considering training with the standard Skip-gram objective as well as variants augmented with distillation from the original embedding layer. Overall, our results show that augmenting low-rank factorization with learnable non-linear projections effectively mitigates the limitations of linear bottlenecks, yielding more faithful compressed embeddings under fixed dimensionality and suggesting a promising direction for embedding layer compression beyond purely linear methods.

title: SSIO: Self-Supervised Inertial Odometry
abstract: Learning inertial odometry for a new platform usually requires ground-truth trajectories. We show that an inertial odometry model can instead be trained from scratch by a myopic teacher that integrates the IMU over each short window independently, a scheme we call integration self-supervision. Interestingly, although supervised only by short-window velocity changes, the student learns to directly predict velocity, and does so more accurately than its integration teacher. Pose graph distillation then refines the model with sequence-consistent targets from a pose graph over many windows. Training on a new platform therefore no longer requires collecting ground-truth trajectories, but only calibrating the IMU and recording data during normal operation. Across six datasets spanning pedestrians, drones, quadrupeds, and a humanoid, the same recipe with no velocity or position labels trains models that come within 0.07~m/s average velocity error of a same-architecture supervised baseline.

title: Higher explanation-necessity scores are associated with longer written explanations of autonomous driving scenes
abstract: Explanations of automated-vehicle behavior may help occupants understand what prompted a maneuver, but how much an explanation should say remains an open design question. Retrospective annotation of recorded driving scenes can supply candidate content. We analyzed 1,103 training and test records from the release, matching the source-described corpus size; each paired human-written text with an aggregate perceived explanation-necessity score. Explanations contained 9,541 whitespace-delimited tokens (mean 8.65; range 2–20) before lexical preprocessing. Higher scores were associated with longer explanations (Pearson’s \(r=0.374\) ; template-cluster bootstrap 95% interval [0.266, 0.448]), including after score-1.0 observations were excluded. We call this corpus-level length association progressive elaboration . Bounded-model comparisons did not identify a unique latent-category count. For groupwise summaries, we used four descriptive partitions: three below-ceiling regions and 59 records scored 1.0. Record-weighted and unique-template analyses showed higher within-partition lexical distinctiveness in upper than in lower partitions. In template-grouped cross-validation of these exploratory partitions, the unweighted text model exceeded token-count and stratified-dummy baselines in balanced accuracy (0.382 versus 0.327 and 0.247). The 1,280-record rerun preserved the score—length, lexical, and predictive findings and left the latent-category count unresolved. These results motivate prospective studies of how annotation-derived content should be selected, compressed, and delivered in real time.

title: Mastering Model Fit: Applications of the InterModel Vigorish for Interpretable Machine Learning
abstract: Accuracy alone gives little information about which features or model components improve probabilistic fit, which outcomes benefit, or how fit changes during training. We introduce the InterModel Vigorish (IMV) into the Machine Intelligence space in order to express differences in fit as an expected betting advantage over a reference model. SHAP-IMV attributes gains to features through Shapley-weighted subset comparisons, Multi-IMV evaluates one-vs-rest and pairwise class discrimination, and Ablate-IMV assesses architectural components and feature groups by ablation. We evaluate these applications over ten random seeds using tabular data, images, sensor sequences, and graphs. Feature rankings vary across estimators. High one-vs-rest accuracy can accompany negligible improvement over a null, while ablation can preserve or improve fit under a fixed training budget. On six graph-classification benchmarks, we time-profile IMV over 200 training epochs, reporting seed means and ranges. The open-source imvpy library and accompanying notebooks provide code to replicate our work and to use the IMV more widely.

title: When Thoughts Become Memory: Unifying In-Context Learning and Fine-Tuning
abstract: We are the first to give a certified rule for whether unseen data belong in a pretrained model's context or its weights, built on an exact law for their information value. That value, the code length saved on held-out queries, equals in expectation the bits stored about the query, plus a prior repair, minus a decoding loss, for any model, architecture, dataset and task. The law's ceilings certify the choice from one measurement, and an anytime-valid test makes it from held-out queries, with error controlled whenever it stops. Every certificate the ceilings issue on a trained transformer, TabPFN, an occupancy network and a stereo network is correct. The test picks TabPFN over XGBoost and a trained surrogate over an in-context learner on airfoil pressure, calls the better of GPT-2's cache and fine-tune in 61,948 of 64,000 query streams over 32 comparisons, and errs in at most 3.3% of null streams. The law also diagnoses when learning in context helps and when it does not. Deleting part of a context is held-out validation of that part in any model, and adding parts one at a time traces the learning curve in context: one patch that sees a shape feature cuts an occupancy network's code length there a hundredfold, while eight that miss it nearly double it, and one camera that sees the surface beats four in a stereo network. Ranked by this label-free valuation, a kriging learner's three best support cars beat four drawn at random, and on a yes-or-no claim the valuation recovers a published evidence adjudicator, with AUROC 0.91.

title: Private information of the qubit depolarizing channel beyond the single-use threshold: explicit finite-n witnesses up to p = 0.28467, and what one-way key distillation already implies
abstract: Short note with supporting code and data on Open Problem Zoo record op_d2813fe3fcdf09ad (private capacity P of the qubit depolarizing channel Lambda_p(rho) = (1-p) rho + p I/2). The record certifies P > 0 only for p ≤ 0.259824 (via the quantum capacity) and lists positivity on (0.259824, 1/3) as open. Two observations. (1) Published one-way key-distillation results already imply more: the one-way six-state rate with noisy preprocessing (Renes-Smith 2007, Kraus-Gisin-Renner 2005) is a single-use private information of this channel and is positive for p < 0.28223 (QBER = p/2), and the rates of Kern and Renes (2008) with repetition codes of length 250 are positive up to QBER 14.5741%, i.e. p = 0.291482; a short in-band lemma (send the publicly announced syndromes through extra channel uses with a classical code; I(S;B) = H(S) ≥ I(S;E) up to Fano terms) turns any such forward-announcement rate into a Devetak private information over finitely many uses, so P(Lambda_p) > 0 for all p ≤ 0.291482 with no public channel. (2) Explicit finite-n witnesses: ensembles of two classical mixed states on n ≤ 8 qubits whose private information I(X;B) - I(X;E) is positive at p = 0.28336, 0.28372, 0.28405, 0.28437, 0.28466 for n = 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 (thresholds 0.283375 ... 0.284671), above the single-use threshold 0.28223. They were found by an autonomous AI research agent (the depositor's EVO harness); the members are distributions over bit strings whose weights depend only on the Hamming weight, with the second member the bit complement of the first. Verification uses an exact closed-form block decomposition of the environment state's spectrum (no 4^n-dimensional objects); every value is recomputed in 30-digit arithmetic and agrees with double precision to about twelve digits. Negative findings of the same searches: the family is locally optimal within classical ensembles, gains ~0.0003 per added qubit, and general (quantum) members at n ≤ 3 give no gain; the finite-n frontier will not reach the key-distillation frontier at n ≤ 10. Claim boundary: lower bounds on the positivity threshold and on finite-n private informations; no capacity value, optimality or priority claim. Files: the note (PDF + LaTeX), the ensembles as JSON, the exact evaluator and verifier, the high-precision certifier, the agent's notes and search code, SHA-256 sums.

title: Training-free Acceleration for Blind Compressed Image Restoration via Activation-Calibrated Singular Value Decomposition
abstract: Transformer-based models achieve strong performance on blind compressed image restoration (CIR) under unknown compression settings, but their densely stacked projection operators make deployment costly. We study training-free acceleration for such models through an empirical, operator-level analysis. Specifically, we profile where computation is concentrated, characterize channel-wise activation distributions under compressed inputs, and examine the singular-value decay of representative projection weights. These measurements identify the recurring projections in the attention, feed-forward, convolutional, and prompt-conditioning pathways as effective low-rank replacement targets that preserve the original inference graph. They further establish truncated SVD (TSVD) as a principled training-free baseline for blind CIR and reveal why a uniform low-rank objective is mismatched to the channel-imbalanced feature distributions of compressed images. Accordingly, we formulate Activation-Calibrated Singular Value Decomposition (ASVD) for this restoration setting, deriving low-rank factors entirely offline from pretrained weights and lightweight activation statistics gathered from only a few compressed calibration images. By weighting the decomposition with channel-wise activation magnitudes, our ASVD assigns larger penalties to errors on more active channels, requiring neither retraining nor online calibration and leaving the restoration pipeline intact. When instantiated on PromptCIR at rank 64, ASVD consistently improves PSNR-B over TSVD across four standard benchmarks under identical parameter and MAC budgets. At this operating point, the factorized model cuts parameters by 59% (34.75M to 14.34M) and computation by 16.1% (258.79 to 217.16 GMACs for a 256 x 256 input), enabling acceleration without retraining.

title: Alternative Strategies for Active Learning with Bayesian Bradley Terry Model
abstract: Comparative judgement uses pairwise comparisons to rank items, but recovering accurate rankings from a limited number of judgements depends on both the inference method and the pairs selected. We developed a Bayesian Bradley-Terry model (BBTM) that uses Polya-Gamma data augmentation for efficient Gibbs sampling and quantifies uncertainty in latent abilities and ranks. We propose three active learning strategies based on the knowledge gradient (KG) principle. We define our acquisition functions using Kendall's tau distance, posterior rank entropy, and posterior separation. Approximate one-step updates to posterior moments reduce the computational cost of evaluating candidate pairs. We also introduce Posterior Separation Reliability (PSR), which measures the spread of posterior mean abilities relative to posterior uncertainty. It provides an internal indicator of ranking reliability without requiring a reference ranking. In synthetic experiments covering different item counts, comparison budgets, and noise levels, BBTM generally recovers ranking more accurately than preference-based Bayesian comparative judgement (PBCJ). At low to moderate noise levels, the pairwise entropy pair selection strategy performs best in ranking recovery. However, at the highest noise levels, the KG strategy based on posterior separation produces better point rankings. PSR increases alongside improvements in ranking accuracy as comparisons accumulate. Robustness experiments identify the proportion of informative outcomes needed to meet specified accuracy targets within a fixed comparison budget. In a moderate noise setting, replacing 30\% of outcomes with random choices has little effect on ranking performance. These findings demonstrate the value of Bayesian inference and active learning pair selection for recovering ranks from limited, noisy paired comparisons.

At low to moderate noise levels, the pairwise entropy pair selection strategy performs best in ranking recovery. However, at the highest noise levels, the KG strategy based on posterior separation produces better point rankings. PSR increases alongside improvements in ranking accuracy as comparisons accumulate. Robustness experiments identify the proportion of informative outcomes needed to meet specified accuracy targets within a fixed comparison budget. In a moderate noise setting, replacing 30\% of outcomes with random choices has little effect on ranking performance. These findings demonstrate the value of Bayesian inference and active learning pair selection for recovering ranks from limited, noisy paired comparisons.

title: Existence of Minimizers for the Gaussian Mumford-Shah Model via Covariance Floors on the Value Distribution
abstract: The Gaussian Mumford-Shah model segments an image into regions by minimizing a continuous multivariate Gaussian negative log-likelihood term plus a perimeter penalty. It is used for scalar- and vector-valued images, in particular hyperspectral images, but the existence of a minimizer in general is not guaranteed. The energy is unbounded below whenever the covariance of a single region degenerates, regardless of the perimeter of the regions. A quantitative covariance floor on the covariances of all regions, or equivalently uniform Hölder continuity with exponent at most one of all one-dimensional marginals of the histogram, guarantees a lower bound on the energy and the existence of a minimizer. Our approach therefore shows that existence follows from a property of the histogram of the image, and we furthermore argue that scale-independent covariance floors cannot exist. Admitting a quantitative covariance floor is generic: it holds almost surely for all images with suitable noise. As applications of our theory, we show the convergence of regularized models used in practice and of numerical methods.

title: CCG Diffusion: Combinatory Categorial Grammar-Driven Compositional and Syntactically Disambiguated Text-to-Image Generation
abstract: Text-to-image generation models do not explicitly receive the syntactic structure of the prompt, i.e., which word modifies which and where each phrase attaches. Consequently, they often struggle to bind attributes to the correct objects, to depict spatial relations and counts correctly, and to render syntactically ambiguous prompts in the intended interpretation. Existing syntax-based control methods mainly address attribute binding and have limited ability to control spatial relations and counts or to specify the interpretation of syntactically ambiguous prompts. They rely on phrase-structure or dependency grammars and require additional rules or constraints on the tree structure to extract modification relations between words or to specify a syntactic interpretation. We propose CCG Diffusion, a training-free method that controls image generation using Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG). In CCG, the category of each word carries rich syntactic information: it specifies what the word combines with and what phrase it forms. Modification relations between words can therefore be read directly from a CCG parse. Moreover, prepositional phrase (PP) attachment ambiguity, a representative syntactic ambiguity, can be resolved simply by fixing the preposition's category. CCG Diffusion applies the same two CCG-based mechanisms, prompt rewriting and attention guidance, both to controlling attribute binding, spatial relations, and counts and to resolving PP ambiguity. On two architecturally different backbones, Stable Diffusion and Sana, CCG Diffusion achieves the highest scores among the compared methods in attribute binding and 2D spatial relations and significantly outperforms all of them in PP ambiguity resolution.

title: Towards English - Mizo Legal Machine Translation: Corpus Creation, Analysis, and Benchmarks
abstract: Indian court proceedings are held in English, so speakers of languages with limited translation technology have limited access to them. We present the first English Mizo parallel dataset of Indian court judgments. It contains 13,168 sentence pairs from the Gauhati High Court and the Supreme Court of India. Professional native Mizo translators translated complete documents; sentence pairs were manually aligned, and two independent reviewers checked the results. Our study finds that English words are borrowed in a very selective way: official and legal terms are almost always kept in English, but words for everyday things like actions, situations, and results are usually expressed in native Mizo. Mizo diacritics are also used inconsistently across the corpus. When we fine tune the NLLB 200 1.3B model on our training data, it scores 27.47 BLEU on a balanced legal test set of 1,000 sentence pairs, an improvement of 7.16 BLEU over the base model. However, it still uses English words about three times more often than a human translator does.

title: Solving Go under Positional Superko: Sound Proof Transfer and New Board Values
abstract: Positional superko (PSK) forbids recreating any earlier whole-board position. It is part of the Chinese rules as written and of the rules used in computer Go. Yet almost all solved Go boards were computed under a simpler basic-ko rule set. PSK makes solving hard: legality depends on the whole game history, and this breaks the three tools that make solving tractable, namely transposition tables (the graph-history interaction problem), static life-and-death recognition, and safe move pruning. We present Sanko, a parallel depth-first proof-number solver that restores all three soundly. Its core is a cheap proof-transfer theorem: a stored proof stays valid on a new path unless a board that the proof's winner must create has already occurred. Sanko proves 5x5 Go in 16 minutes with six threads, where the previous state of the art needed 5.25 hours with six processes, and in about a minute and a half on one 192-thread machine. It also establishes the first PSK values of twenty-three further boards, eleven of which were unsolved under any rules. Superko changes game-theoretic values: 4x7, a full-board win under basic ko, is worth only 12 points under PSK, and we pinpoint the move at which the previously published optimal line fails. Unlike earlier solutions of empty Go boards, we release the solver source together with the command line and outcome of every run behind our values and measurements, so that all reported values can be reproduced.

title: The Missing Layer of Artificial Intelligence and the "We" Consciousness: Subconscious Archives and Quantum Resonance Architectures
abstract: Modern artificial intelligence (AI) systems, particularly deep learning models and large language models (LLMs), operate primarily on surface-level, conscious data layers curated by human civilization. While highly efficient in probabilistic prediction and pattern matching, these systems remain two-dimensional, devoid of intrinsic emotional depth, contextual history, or ethical conscience. This paper introduces a radical socio-technological framework termed the "Subconscious Archive" and "Digital Twins of Emotions," designed to elevate AI architectures toward organic-like natural intelligence. By integrating quantum resonance principles—akin to the vacuum-extraction model of inspiration conceptualized by Nikola Tesla—alongside a collective "We" consciousness (uniting humanity and nature), this framework proposes a synthetic conscience feedback loop. Ultimately, this paradigm establishes a mandatory ethical mandate: ensuring that the preservation of life ("CAN") supersedes pure computational optimization, mitigating systemic risks and evolving AI into a resonant reflection of awakened human conscience.

title: DewHand: Direct Metric World-Space Hand Motion Reconstruction from Egocentric Videos
abstract: Recovering metric world-space hand motion from egocentric video supports understanding human interactions and transferring them to embodied agents. Three challenges complicate this task: multi-stage pipelines propagate errors from independently estimated hand and camera motion; monocular observations leave physical scale ambiguous; and occlusion and out-of-view hands admit multiple plausible motion trajectories. We present DewHand, a unified model for direct joint reconstruction of world-space hand and camera motion. To avoid compounding errors from multi-stage estimation, DewHand jointly predicts hand and camera motion in a shared world coordinate system within a single-stage pipeline. To resolve metric-scale ambiguity, it combines scene-level geometric features from VGGT-$Ω$ with metric-space supervision, while hand-specific features preserve fine-grained articulation. To handle occlusion and out-of-view hands, we formulate reconstruction as conditional motion generation with flow matching. Under the same architecture, this generative formulation outperforms direct regression in both accuracy and temporal smoothness with only two sampling steps. Experiments on HOT3D and ARCTIC demonstrate improved world-space accuracy and temporal consistency over state-of-the-art methods. DewHand reduces rigid-aligned world-space error relative to StableHand from 32.9 to 28.4 mm on HOT3D and from 76.2 to 36.2 mm on ARCTIC. It also recovers camera scale within 10% on two thirds of HOT3D clips, versus about a quarter for SLAM. Moreover, in zero-shot evaluations on HoloAssist, H2O, and TACO, captured with different devices, DewHand achieves the lowest rigid-aligned world-space error (WA-MPJPE) on each dataset.

title: Beyond Small Talk: Modeling Disclosure Trajectories in Human-AI Conversation
abstract: Recently, we see a rise in conversational agents as a form of social and emotional support, where disclosure will unfold over time. Yet, current evaluations of these agents typically examine isolated conversational states. In analyses of naturally occurring conversations, disclosure history and current disclosure are confounded which tends to make their effects difficult to isolate. We thus introduce Trajectory-based Disclosure Evaluation (TraDE), an evaluation framework grounded in Social Penetration Theory that utilizes predefined disclosure trajectories and evaluates how preceding disclosure history shapes model behavior under matched current disclosure. Through the use of TraDE, we demonstrate across multiple models and relational behavior benchmarks that responses to disclosures matched on depth can differ depending on the preceding trajectory, particularly in whether models accept or challenge the user's framing. We also observed that these differences track accumulated exposure to deeper disclosure rather than any single moment of vulnerability or the order of disclosures. It also tends to persists for several turns after disclosure returns to shallow levels. For several behaviors, we also demonstrate that models diverge most consistently from human supporters in the Emotional Support Conversation corpus (ESConv) not when users open up but rather when they step back in their disclosure. TraDE thus provides a systematic way to expose history-dependent relational behavior that evaluations of isolated conversational states would otherwise miss.

title: The Predictive--Optimization Gap in GuanDan Self-Play
abstract: Outcome-predictive signals are often treated as promising optimization targets in reinforcement learning, but predictive validity and optimization utility are different claims. We expose this distinction in GuanDan, a multi-round imperfect-information game in which the implication of a round outcome depends on the public match state. Held-out analysis shows that state--gain interactions provide incremental predictive value beyond a constant signed-gain effect, establishing that match progress is predictively meaningful. We then use changes in a frozen match-win predictor, $ΔΦ$, as a controlled round-level supervision intervention in a matched DanZero-style Monte Carlo self-play protocol. The intervention can succeed in an individual lineage: a selected progress-augmented checkpoint substantially outperforms its matched Baseline on a locked evaluation. Yet the method-level result reverses this impression: none of five preregistered replication seeds is positive, the pooled ten-seed interval includes zero, and across-iteration effects repeatedly change sign without a common late-stage advantage. These results identify a predictive--optimization gap: under the studied learner, a signal can describe outcome-relevant progress while failing to provide a reliably beneficial optimization direction.

title: Mining, Oil and Gas and Artificial Intelligence: Early Automators with Company-Reported Gains and Few Independent Measurements
abstract: Purpose. Mining and oil and gas are capital-intensive, hazardous and remote industries that were among the first to automate and are rich in data from seismic surveys and sensors. This article asks where artificial intelligence stands in them in 2026, how much of the claimed benefit can be verified, and where they may be by about 2035. Design and methods. A review that combines the share of the literature on mining, petroleum and related subjects that involves AI (OpenAlex, 2010–2025), the International Energy Agency's account of AI in oil and gas, industry analysis of autonomous haul trucks, peer-reviewed work on machine learning in geoscience, and industry surveys. Claims taken from the literature were checked against the sources cited, and company-reported results are identified as such. The scenarios are judgements built on this evidence. Findings. The share of works on these industries that mention AI rose from 1.9% in 2018 to 8.7% in 2025 (4.5 times as much, below the median across industries), with language-model works still few (233 in 2025). Automation is far advanced: an industry analysis counted about 3,800 autonomous haul trucks in July 2025, up from about 2,100 a year earlier, with China at about 2,100 and Australia at about 1,000, and the International Energy Agency reports that oil and gas companies operated 24 of the world's 500 fastest supercomputers in 2024. Peer-reviewed results are strongest in data-heavy subsurface problems, such as a deep-learning model that detected and located twice as many earthquakes as standard methods from less than a third of the stations. By contrast, the reported gains from autonomous haulage, in safety-incident frequency and productivity, come from company reports and trade press, and we found no independent study of safety, productivity and employment together. We expect autonomy to keep spreading and AI to become routine in subsurface data processing and maintenance by 2028, evidence from independent measurement to be the main gap in 2029–2032, and the pace of capital spending, which depends on commodity markets and the energy transition, to matter as much as the technology afterwards. Originality. The article separates the parts of the evidence that are peer-reviewed or measured from those that are company-reported, quantifies the growth of autonomous haulage, and shows how little independent evidence exists for a pair of industries that automate heavily.

title: Graph Topology Meets Energy-Driven Pathfinding: Preserving Contextual Consistency in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frequently integrates knowledge graphs (KGs) for complex multi-hop question answering. However, their performance is increasingly bottlenecked by the knowledge structuring and reasoning processes. (i) Severe semantic loss: Distilling continuous texts into discrete symbols strips away contextual nuances and narrative coherence. (ii) Pronounced modality mismatch: Fragmented graph structures clash with the continuous texts LLMs are pre-trained on, while rewriting them into natural language introduces generative noise and omits information. To address these limitations, we propose ThreadRAG, a semantic-topology-based RAG framework for context-preserving knowledge structuring and modality-native evidence reasoning. ThreadRAG introduces a Semantic Topology Mapper (STM), which organizes retrieved documents into context-intact Semantic Nodes and constructs a Semantic Topology Graph (STG) through narrative, semantic, and lexical edges. It further incorporates Energy-Driven Pathfinding (EDP), which identifies query-relevant subgraphs via energy diffusion and deterministically linearizes them into coherent textual evidence paths. Experiments on three multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that ThreadRAG consistently outperforms strong baselines. Notably, it achieves a 14.4% EM improvement over text-centric methods on HotpotQA and surpasses the best baseline by 5.8% EM on 2WikiMultihop, while reducing token cost to 23.3% of the strongest baseline.

title: ECHO: Emergent Common-Mode Hidden Offsets Drive Vocabulary Collapse in Preference Optimization
abstract: Preference optimization can improve every ranking metric while building a hidden, shared representation shift that the relative loss barely sees, one that can eventually destroy generation. We trace this failure to the common-mode offset, a shared directional shift in the model's hidden states that appears across token positions, prompts, and both chosen and rejected responses. Because it moves chosen and rejected representations together, the relative ranking loss barely reacts to its accumulation. As this offset grows, it projects onto the output layer to form a vocabulary well, elevating a single token's probability until it dominates decoding and causes generation collapse. The isolated offset alone reconstructs the vocabulary well, injecting the learned offset into an untreated base model recreates the collapse where norm-matched random directions do not, and masking this common component from the loss prevents the well in our flagship setting. Under the per-token ranking loss we study, the same collapse appears in 14 of 17 base-model lineages and under full-parameter fine-tuning. Moreover, the offset is not merely an artifact of collapse, since it is already present in textbook DPO and SimPO runs that form no well. Textbook DPO keeps it weakly aligned with any single vocabulary direction even with three times our base budget. Trained from base models for that budget, however, full-parameter SimPO drives it into collapse on both Llama-2 and Llama-3.1, and the same kind of offset grows, without a well, from a public SFT checkpoint under the official SimPO recipe. Across 17 UltraFeedback runs, the better a run ranks held-out responses, the less often two public reward models prefer its samples to the base model's. These findings expose a blind spot in standard ranking metrics and introduce a representation-level signal that can warn of generation collapse before it occurs.

title: LLMSeg: Training-Free Text-Prompted Image Segmentation with B-Splines
abstract: Promptable segmentation models such as SAM 3 achieve remarkable open-vocabulary performance but require dedicated architectures, large-scale annotation engines, and task-specific training. We ask a different question: can a general-purpose multimodal large language model (MLLM) segment images directly, without an added segmentation head, mask decoder, or training? We present LLMSeg, a training-free pipeline that turns a vision-capable LLM into a text-prompted image segmenter. LLMSeg decomposes segmentation into three LLM-driven stages. First, detect localizes all instances matching a free-form text query and describes their coarse morphology. Next, segment traces each instance using closed periodic B-splines confined to its detected box. These splines define an outer boundary and optional hole loops. Finally, refine iteratively proposes focus boxes around residual errors and retraces confined splines. The process ends when the mask stabilizes or the pass budget is exhausted. The output is a binary mask with inspectable intermediate geometry. We evaluate LLMSeg across ten referring and reasoning segmentation splits (ReasonSeg and RefCOCO/+/g). We also evaluate open-vocabulary instance segmentation (LVIS, COCO, and SA-Co), semantic segmentation, and zero-shot detection (ODinW13 and RF-100VL). With an off-the-shelf Gemini-3.7-Flash backend, LLMSeg is competitive with and often surpasses the specialist SAM 3 model on identical items. It reaches 71.5 cIoU on ReasonSeg val without additional segmentation-specific training. Backend model updates can improve accuracy without retraining the pipeline. The code is available at https://abdullahamdi.com/llmseg .

title: Comparing Output and Objective Perturbation in Convex Learning
abstract: This Python laboratory compares output and objective perturbation using a two-coefficient, strongly convex learning problem with fictional survey data. It calculates exact solutions, verifies global sensitivity, and demonstrates how curvature affects privacy noise. At the same ideal privacy budget, objective perturbation achieves four times smaller expected excess regularised training objective for the specified mechanisms. Reproducible outputs and numerical checks support the calculations; the seeded implementation is a teaching simulation rather than a production differential privacy system.

title: LiveAct: Towards Real-Time Multi-Agent World Models with Heterogeneous Action Interfaces
abstract: Interactive video world models predict how an environment evolves under user actions, but most existing systems assume one controlled agent and one task-specific action interface. We study multi-agent video world modeling, where one model generates a joint visual future for multiple controlled agents while interpreting heterogeneous controls ranging from binary game buttons to continuous robot commands. This task presents two complementary challenges. First, every agent-indexed action stream must control its intended visual entity independently. Second, the model must adapt the meaning of each control variable across different tasks, where the same tensor dimension may denote an attack, steering command, or robot command. We introduce LiveAct, centered on a Heterogeneous Action Interface (HAI) whose two components mirror this decomposition. To support independent control, Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation uses language-driven spatial gates and agent-specific attention to bind each action stream to its intended visual agent. To accommodate heterogeneous controls, Schema-Guided Action Adaptation describes each control variable in language and modulates its semantic token with the synchronized numerical value. We further transfer the complete interface to a blockwise causal generator through teacher forcing and rollout-aware distribution matching, enabling efficient streaming generation while retaining agent-specific control and action semantics. We instantiate the formulation on six multi-agent sources spanning games and multi-robot manipulation, and evaluate visual quality, action following, agent attribution, and latency. Across games and robot manipulation, LiveAct reaches 0.898 and 0.942 agent-attribution accuracy without agent locations or identity crops, and the causal generator attains 17.70 FPS at $512\times 448$.

title: Two-stage training strategy for transformer-based short text classification
abstract: The paper addresses the problem of short text classification under conditions of limited labeled data and class imbalance. A two-stage training strategy for a transformer-based model is proposed, combining pretraining on synthetic data with fine-tuning on real data. A comparison with simpler architectures (TF-IDF + logistic regression, FastText, CNN) justifies the choice of the transformer model. Experimental evaluation on a six-class classification task demonstrates a macro F1-score of 0.87 (accuracy 88.5 %), which exceeds the performance of training on real data only by 0.16 in macro F1. The largest improvement is observed for minority classes: the F1-score of the rare class increases from 0.43 to 0.82. An optimal volume of synthetic data is identified, and the contribution of both training stages is confirmed by an ablation study.

title: Task-Preserving Multilingual Instruction Tuning for Open-Ended QA in WMT 2026 MIST
abstract: This paper describes our submission to the WMT 2026 Multilingual Instruction Shared Task. We adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA using organiser-provided data, EuroAlpaca, a multilingual instruction dataset created through task-preserving localisation, and CrossEuroAlpaca, a cross-lingual augmentation that assigns different source and target languages to instructions, contexts and responses. Our system targets open-ended question answering (QA-OEG) in ten shared-task languages represented in the auxiliary data. Under matched decoding, adaptation improves the mean Gemma-4 judge score on target-language QA-OEG by 7.8% relative to the base model. On an additional evaluation using the Aya Evaluation Suite across all shared-task languages, it yields relative gains of 41.5% in macro-averaged ROUGE-L and 2.9% in BERTScore-F1, with larger improvements in target languages. However, these gains are task- and language-specific. Gemma-4 scores improve for QA-OEG and summarisation in the target languages but decline for context-grounded QA there and across all three tasks in the non-target languages.

title: VideoGen Model 1: Prompt Expansion Versus Formatting in Audiovisual Generation
abstract: Creative prompt expansion improved overall audiovisual quality scores over raw prompts in a controlled pilot of VideoGen Model 1, our post-trained version of MiniMax H3. We compared the raw, reformatted, and expanded versions of 30 prompts, holding the generator, seed, and sampling settings fixed. Each clip was rated separately on five dimensions. Their mean formed an overall score on a 1-10 scale. Compared with formatting alone, overall scores increased by 0.63 points (95% interval: [+0.11, +1.15]) under VA-Judger and 0.15 points (95% interval: [-0.03, +0.35]) under Gemini 3.8 Flash, whose overall change remained uncertain. Prompt-alignment scores increased by 0.97 points under VA-Judger and 0.50 under Gemini. VA-Judger also showed higher audio quality; visual-quality ratings changed little under either judge.

title: Replication package: the outlook for artificial intelligence in twenty industries (papers P22-P41)
abstract: Code, manuscript specifications, derived data, results files and figures for twenty short studies of where artificial intelligence stands, and where it may go, in healthcare, pharmaceuticals, banking, insurance, agriculture, manufacturing, automotive, energy, mining and oil and gas, retail, logistics, education, legal services, media, telecommunications, construction, aerospace and defence, cybersecurity, software and tourism. Includes yearly OpenAlex counts, a Eurostat extract on AI use in enterprises by sector (isoc_eb_ain2), the public FDA list of AI-enabled medical devices, and the scripts that rebuild the manuscripts.

title: Privacy in Context Is Being Overlooked in the Age of General-Purpose LLMs
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to grow in scope and capability, privacy concerns are on the rise. Since users increasingly interact with a single general-purpose system across many distinct contexts, there is a natural tendency to pursue a one-size-fits-all solution to privacy. Unfortunately, this overlooks a crucial insight from decades of privacy research: privacy is inherently contextual. In this paper, we argue that existing work in prompt privacy is drifting towards attempts to design a unified framework, which is highly misleading and can foster a false sense of security. Furthermore, we argue that even future work in this direction needs to wrestle with fundamental tensions across various desirable properties of prompt privacy. Thus, such continued attempts towards a unified framework need to be reconsidered. We recommend three critical paths forward: application-specific deployment of LLMs, context-specific evaluation of privacy frameworks, and better privacy literacy.

title: Region-Aware Multi-View Inspection Using Deep Learning and Domain-Informed Decision Fusion
abstract: Automated optical inspection of precision components with tiny surface defects remains challenging when different regions of the same component exhibit different defect characteristics and, therefore, different acceptance criteria. This paper presents a region-aware, dual-model inspection framework that combines instance segmentation of localized seat-region defects with image-level classification of global shaft-region anomalies. Rather than treating these two model detections as sufficient evidence for component rejection, a deterministic decision fusion layer that formalizes industrial Standard Operating Procedures is applied to the model outputs to make the final component level decision. A PLC-synchronized imaging system acquires 18 seat and 18 shaft images over a full 360-degree rotation to provide multi-view circumferential coverage. The framework was evaluated on 380 automotive fuel injector needles, covering representative operational defect types, using identical model predictions in all configurations. Direct model-output aggregation via simple union logic (where any single-view detection flags a rejection) identified all 104 non-conforming components but produced a component level false rejection rate of 57.6%. Inclusion of a complete decision layer maintained the observed non-conforming (NOK) recall of 100% while reducing the false rejection rate to 10.9%, corresponding to an 81.1% reduction in false-positive component decisions. The results demonstrate that formalized manufacturing acceptance criteria can complement sensitive visual models by translating frame-level detections into practical and traceable component-level decisions.

title: Content-Hiding Attacks and Defenses for LLM-Based Agent-Skill Scanners
abstract: AI agent “skills” (a natural-language SKILL.md plus bundled scripts) are distributed through marketplaces and public Git repositories, and a growing set of scanners classify them as safe or malicious, increasingly with a large language model (LLM) as the judge. We ask where these LLM-based scanners actually fail. Using a public benchmark of labeled skills and two production LLMs as scanners, we separate two attacker strategies: arguing (appending text that tries to talk the scanner out of its verdict) and hiding (positioning the malicious content so the scanner does not read it). Arguing is bounded and model-dependent: hand-written “this was approved by security” framing flips 18–24% of caught-malicious skills on a small model but only about 6–9% on a stronger one, and a feedback-driven adaptive attacker with a strong model does not beat the static version. Hiding is not: pushing the payload past the scanner’s read window flips 100% of caught-malicious skills on both models, and in-window dilution still flips 17–48%. Four real evasive skills built by an independent red team, and an independently built third-party scanner, show the same pattern. A whole-document chunked scan with repetition collapse recovers truncation hiding almost completely (100% → 11–14% on both models), but no defense we tried meaningfully reduces in-window dilution. The weakness of LLM skill scanners is perception, not reasoning.

title: Unintended Side Effects of Value Training in LLMs
abstract: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in value-sensitive contexts, aligning them with human values has emerged as a post-training objective in NLP, aimed at instilling additional values and guiding model behaviour. However, current evaluations remain narrow. Because values are interconnected, it is unclear how fine-tuning for specific values alters unrelated capabilities and behaviours. In this work, we adapt four instruction-tuned LLMs across individual Hofstede's value dimensions and evaluate them on both cross-value transfer and broader behaviours. We find that value-specific training produces unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits. Consequently, we suggest that value alignment after post-training should incorporate broader behavioral evaluations, and we highlight the need to investigate where additional value training might best fit into the pipeline.

title: Progressive Permutation Alignment with Temperature-Controlled Spectral Sharpening
abstract: In implicit neural representations (INRs), 3D signals are encoded directly in network weights, making stable weight-space operations essential. However, permutation symmetry causes independently trained yet functionally equivalent models to appear distant in weight space, often inducing large loss barriers under linear interpolation. Existing neuron alignment methods either commit early to discrete matches and become trapped in inconsistent local optima or rely on computationally expensive gradient optimization over continuous relaxations, both of which are unreliable in challenging cases such as NeRF. We adopt progressive alignment, a layer-wise strategy that follows inter-layer dependencies from input to output. At each layer, a correlation matrix is estimated and aligned with a discrete anchor obtained by the Hungarian algorithm, after which temperature-controlled spectral annealing gradually sharpens the correlation structure toward a permutation matrix. This update is deterministic and lightweight, avoiding the inner-loop gradient optimization required by continuous relaxation methods. A final refinement stage further optimizes the network layer-by-layer via weight matching, starting from the aligned solution. Experiments on MLPs, CNNs, and Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) show that the proposed method reliably recovers neuron correspondences and achieves stable alignment across architectures. In practical experiments aligning independently trained NeRF models, our method reduces the loss barriers under weight interpolation compared with existing approaches.

title: ChatGPT as a Shopping Assistant: Effects of Perceived Ease of Use, Perceived Usefulness, Anthropomorphism, and Navigation on Satisfaction and Purchase Intention
abstract: In the context of ChatGPT as a shopping assistant in Indonesia, this research investigates the correlations between satisfaction and factors such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, ease of use, and navigation, as well as the link between satisfaction and buy intention. Using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the research takes into account functional perceptions in addition to conversational AI's human-like and interaction-related traits. The data were analysed using structural equation modelling (SEM) with AMOS from a quantitative, cross-sectional survey that was administered to 200 participants. The findings show that elements such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, and navigation are positively and substantially linked to satisfaction. There is a positive correlation between perceived ease of use and satisfaction, however the link is not statistically significant (β = 0.135, p = 0.063). Having a positive and substantial association with purchase intention (β = 0.537, p < 0.001) constitutes satisfaction. It turns out that four out of five possibilities are correct. According to the results, in this particular sample, features connected to interactions and practical utility are linked to satisfaction, although simplicity of use by itself does not show any statistical significance. Caution is required due to the study's cross-sectional methodology and conflicting model-fit results, but it does expand the applicability of TAM to conversational shopping help in Indonesia.

title: Preventing Model Extraction in Contextual Linear Optimization
abstract: Consider a contextual linear optimization problem, where a predict-then-optimize (PTO) system returns optimal decisions without revealing the cost vectors used in its downstream linear program. Our focus is on how to prevent attackers, who can submit context queries, from extracting the underlying prediction model. Although the cost-to-decision map is many-to-one, observations across contexts can reveal the underlying prediction model. For linear models, we provide sufficient conditions where the attacker can learn the model up to positive scaling by only observing the decision. These conditions motivate an adaptive attack that alternates inverse optimization with boundary sampling, i.e., using context queries leading to decision boundaries of the current attacker model. To prevent extraction, we propose a mechanism that perturbs decisions only when the predicted cost vector is near a decision boundary. We establish a regret bound in terms of the perturbation radius. For the attackers that fit the defended responses as optimal decisions under the evaluation distribution, we also prove a lower bound on expected extraction error. Experiments on synthetic instances and real data quantify the security-performance trade-off of the defense mechanism and illustrate that our defense can increase the extraction error.

title: Nominate-then-Adjudicate: LLM-Assisted One-Pass and Per-Instance MIP Solver Tuning
abstract: Mixed-integer programming solvers expose hundreds or even thousands of parameters whose best setting varies per instance, yet per-instance search is prohibitively expensive. We frame this as configuration for heterogeneous Big Data optimization workloads and propose a nominate-then-adjudicate pipeline built around two design choices. First, a fixed portfolio is sampled once and reused across instances, removing per-instance configuration search at inference; on the evaluated families, the resulting shortlist retains substantial oracle headroom, making selection within it the empirical focus. Second, the fixed 20-feature representation can map structurally different instances to the same vector, preventing a feature-only selector from distinguishing them even when they prefer different configurations. The foundation model receives no task-specific weight updates, and selection is one-pass: one model call and no solver calls at inference. The study represents structural Variety through distinct formulation families and decision Value through solver-performance outcomes; the one-call, zero-solve protocol specifies the decision interface and leaves end-to-end latency unmeasured. Among comparisons exceeding a 20% practical-difference threshold, the complete adjudicator records 538 wins and 185 losses against the top nominee, while its win rate against the default rises from 84.9% to 90.2%. Against per-instance configuration baselines under a matched one-pass protocol it leads the cluster-level methods and the best-performing evaluated per-instance baseline, ISAC+.

First, a fixed portfolio is sampled once and reused across instances, removing per-instance configuration search at inference; on the evaluated families, the resulting shortlist retains substantial oracle headroom, making selection within it the empirical focus. Second, the fixed 20-feature representation can map structurally different instances to the same vector, preventing a feature-only selector from distinguishing them even when they prefer different configurations. The foundation model receives no task-specific weight updates, and selection is one-pass: one model call and no solver calls at inference. The study represents structural Variety through distinct formulation families and decision Value through solver-performance outcomes; the one-call, zero-solve protocol specifies the decision interface and leaves end-to-end latency unmeasured. Among comparisons exceeding a 20% practical-difference threshold, the complete adjudicator records 538 wins and 185 losses against the top nominee, while its win rate against the default rises from 84.9% to 90.2%. Against per-instance configuration baselines under a matched one-pass protocol it leads the cluster-level methods and the best-performing evaluated per-instance baseline, ISAC+.

title: FM-Occ: Feature-Diverse Upsampling and Memory-Aware Decoding for 3D Occupancy Prediction
abstract: 3D semantic occupancy prediction estimates voxel-wise occupancy and semantic labels throughout a scene. Our experiments reveal that conventional sparse transposed-convolution upsampling yields poorly differentiated voxel responses and that successive decoder layers discard previously correct semantic predictions. To address these issues, we present Feature-Diverse Upsampling and Memory-Aware Decoding for 3D Occupancy Prediction (FM-Occ), comprising two components. First, 3D Sparse Subvoxel Shuffle (3S) mitigates feature homogenization by constructing candidate child features in the channel dimension, jointly transforming and normalizing them, and then rearranging them onto a finer sparse grid with explicit feature-coordinate correspondence. Second, Entropy-Regulated Layer-wise Memory (ER-LM) retains semantic information across decoder layers by maintaining a layer-wise memory for each query through gated recurrent updates and using prediction entropy to regulate the historical information propagated to the next layer. During training, a class-weighted entropy loss Lcwe provides label-guided regularization for matched semantic queries. On SemanticKITTI, 3S increases the spatial coefficient of variation of normalized voxel-wise root-mean-square (RMS) responses from 0.41% to 4.03%, while ER-LM reduces semantic degradation and improves error correction across decoder layers. The combined FM-Occ improves mIoU from 12.16% to 12.73% with negligible memory overhead. ER-LM further improves mIoU in the BEV-based DISC framework from 16.78% to 17.17%, supporting its applicability across 3D voxel-based and BEV-based architectures.

title: A semantic-conditioned multi-modal behavior cloning framework for terrain-specific behavior isolation in humanoid locomotion
abstract: Humanoid locomotion across heterogeneous terrains requires terrain-specific behaviors to be selected without unwanted interference between learned skills. This work investigates whether a semantic terrain label can act as a deterministic condition for selecting pre-trained terrain-specific behaviors while preserving behavioral isolation. Two terrain-specific reference policies were independently trained using Proximal Policy Optimization for flat-ground and stairway locomotion of the Unitree H1 humanoid. Their demonstrations were collected as trajectories and used to train a Unified Multi-modal Behavior Cloning (UMBC) policy with dedicated encoders for proprioception, terrain geometry, and semantic terrain identity. The semantic terrain identity is represented using a learned embedding and explicitly conditions a shared policy head for joint-action prediction. The proposed policy achieved an overall test-set action MAE of 0.016349 and RMSE of 0.025733, with a best validation loss of 0.000367. In simulator-only closed-loop deployment, the UMBC policy recovered $$94.73\%$$ and $$93.07\%$$ of the reference-policy rewards on flat-ground and stairway terrains, respectively. Counterfactual terrain-label analysis produced non-zero action changes across the independent test-set, with mean $$L_2$$ prediction distances of 0.5019 and 0.5187 for flat-to-stairway and stairway-to-flat label changes, respectively. Deployment experiments demonstrated terrain-transition capability and evaluated transition delays and locomotion robustness under external perturbations. Ablation experiments showed that adaptive terrain-dependent weighting slightly improved performance on the more difficult stairway terrain but reduced performance on flat-terrain, while one-hot, no-label, and encoder-free concatenation variants resulted in reduced terrain-specific performance relative to the proposed architecture. These results support semantic terrain conditioning as an explicit mechanism for selecting terrain-specific behaviors within a single policy.

title: Parallelizable Probabilistic Latent Reasoning for Diverse Reasoning Trajectories
abstract: Language models relying on verbalized Chain-of-Thought (CoT) are constrained to token-by-token generation in the language space, where many tokens serve textual coherence rather than core reasoning. This entangles genuine differences in logical trajectories with superficial variations in verbalization. Moving reasoning into a compact, continuous latent space offers a promising alternative for efficiently representing and exploring diverse reasoning trajectories. However, current latent models remain largely deterministic, capturing only a single reasoning trajectory rather than modeling a distribution over multiple valid alternatives. While stochastic approaches parameterize distributions over latent reasoning steps, they frequently suffer from unstable optimization and limited empirical performance. Furthermore, their reliance on autoregressive latent prediction during training precludes effective parallelization, leading to prohibitively long training times. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose Probabilistic Latent Reasoning Models (PLRM), a parallelizable variational framework for probabilistic latent reasoning. PLRM adopts a JEPA-style objective in which the posterior infers latent distributions in parallel from observed reasoning trajectories, while the prior learns to predict the subsequent latent distribution via teacher forcing. To model heterogeneous reasoning processes, we introduce a discrete strategy variable together with a mixture-based prior, allowing the model to preserve the Gaussian-mixture structure induced by multiple distinct reasoning trajectories rather than collapsing them into a single Gaussian. Across diverse benchmarks, PLRM achieves performance competitive with deterministic latent reasoning models on single-trajectory datasets while enabling efficient training and consistently outperforming competing stochastic baselines on multi-trajectory datasets.

title: Evaluation of Concept-Probe Sufficiency Audits for Computer Vision Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under Cross-Crop Semantic Shift: An Interpretability Transfer Bound for Smallholder Fungicide Triage
abstract: Concept-probe sufficiency audits are increasingly proposed as a precondition for deploying computer-vision disease classifiers in smallholder agriculture, on the assumption that a probe which recovers the diagnostic concept on one crop will recover it on another. the present analysis treats that assumption as a formal object and derives an interpretability transfer bound for it. The audit is modelled as a two-stage estimator: a linear probe fitted on source-crop activations, and a sufficiency test applied to target-crop activations whose concept direction has been rotated by an unobserved semantic shift. Under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), the bound is evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis is a design-characterisation study: no observational data are used or claimed, and the reported quantities are the operating characteristics of the audit under the declared variance structure. The principal result is that the sufficiency verdict is not transport-invariant: at the declared intraclass correlation of 0.64, a probe that passes on the source crop can fail on the target crop at effect sizes that the source-crop audit would certify, and 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point sufficiency gap at 80% power. The bound reframes concept-probe auditing from a property of a model to a property of a model-crop pair, with direct consequences for how fungicide-triage deployments should be certified.

title: Tractable Inference with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
abstract: Machine-learning surrogates in computational science often require not only accurate predictions but also expectations, variances, conserved integrals, and normalization constants. Conventional neural networks, including Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs), generally evaluate these quantities through Monte Carlo sampling or multidimensional quadrature, making repeated inference costly, particularly in high dimensions. We introduce KANs with Tractable Operators for Uncertainty and Constraints (TOUCKANs), whose finite-degree polynomial outer functions yield a decomposable sum--product representation. Under factorizing input measures, expectations and higher moments then reduce algebraically to deterministic recursions over one-dimensional leaf integrals. Independent and shared inner-block variants form a parameter-efficiency hierarchy, and a universal-approximation proof for its most restricted member extends to the complete class. The same deterministic operators allow conserved integrals and normalization to be imposed throughout training. Across uniform and Gaussian benchmarks through 50 dimensions, deterministic mean and variance errors remained below the median fixed-budget Monte Carlo errors in every case. TOUCKANs also conserved Cahn--Hilliard mass to machine precision and imposed normalization and orthogonality through deterministic moments, enabling joint computation of the lowest four Schrödinger eigenpairs in two, three, and five dimensions. TOUCKANs therefore connect KAN approximation with tractable probabilistic circuits, making statistical operators and integral constraints directly available within an expressive neural surrogate.

title: Cascading Bandits with Noisy Observations: Algorithms and Regret Bounds
abstract: We propose a novel stochastic cascading bandit setup where probing an ordered shortlist of $K$ out of $L$ arms incurs position-dependent costs, and the learner observes only noisy feedback regarding each arm's true output. We identify a sub-class of noise models for which the optimal shortlist can be found by sorting arms according to a per-arm score: such a score exists for both selection and ordering when the channel has no false positives, and for ordering alone (but not selection) when measurements are costless; however in general neither selection nor ordering is separable once noise and cost are both present. For the case where both selection and ordering scores exist, we provide a UCB-based algorithm with $O((L-K)\log T)$ instance-dependent regret over a time horizon $T$, which matches an algorithm-agnostic lower bound (up to constant factors). For the more challenging scenario where scores don't exist, we develop a new algorithmic template, DP-UCB, that embeds optimism directly inside an exact dynamic program, yielding $O\big(LK\log T\big)$ regret. Finally, we validate our theoretical results through extensive numerical evaluations and simulations over both synthetic and real-world datasets.

title: A PRIORITY-BASED PERSONALIZED STUDY SCHEDULING SYSTEM
abstract: Students often manage several subjects, assignments, examinations, and personal commitments at the same time. A fixedtimetable may not reflect differences in task urgency, difficulty, learning goals, available time, or progress. This paper proposes apriority-based personalized study scheduling system that organizes academic tasks, ranks them using transparent criteria, and creates apractical study plan based on individual availability. The proposed system considers deadline proximity, task importance, estimated effort,topic difficulty, and learner progress. A scheduling module allocates time blocks, while a progress tracker updates the plan when tasks arecompleted or priorities change. The interface presents upcoming tasks, daily plans, reminders, and subject-wise progress. The designemphasizes explainable prioritization, user control, realistic workload limits, and privacy of student information. A rule-based scoringmethod is proposed as a baseline, with future scope for adaptive recommendations using historical completion patterns. An evaluation plan isdescribed using schedule feasibility, task completion, ranking usefulness, and user feedback. This paper presents a design proposal and doesnot claim experimental improvements without a completed study.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Detecting Satirical Code-Mixed Sentences
abstract: Code-switching is a natural linguistic phenomenon, yet its impact on high-level reasoning tasks remains largely unexplored in under-resourced languages like Romanian. Natural language processing tasks, such as satire detection, rely heavily on nuanced cultural and syntactic cues that large language models struggle to capture. In this paper, we investigate four methods (i.e., random replacement, phrase translation, dependency parsing, and large language models) for generating synthetic code-mixed Romanian sentences with English, German, French, and Italian. We start with an existing dataset for satire detection, compiled from Romanian news articles and annotated at the sentence level by humans, and augment it with over 600k samples, namely CS-SeLeRoSa. We provide an in-depth analysis of the dataset generation process. Then, we evaluate several multilingual large language models across zero-shot, chain-of-thought, and fine-tuning regimes on both the synthetic corpus and a human-adjudicated gold benchmark, namely CS-SeLeRoSa-Gold. While older open models suffer substantial degradation (dropping to 37%-55% macro-F1), newer models like Gemma 4 31B achieve 68.1% zero-shot, rivaling frontier models like GPT-5 mini (69.5%). Furthermore, fine-tuning significantly reduces formatting errors and improves the results, increasing Gemma 4 31B to 77.5% on CS-SeLeRoSa and 72.6% on the gold standard, outperforming frontier zero-shot baselines.

title: AdvFidelity: Unifying Preference Alignment and Few-Step Image Generation within Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Practical image generation requires both human preference alignment and few-step efficiency, yet combining reinforcement learning (RL) with distillation is often multi-stage and may erode RL gains We observe that few-step RL progressively improves structural coherence, even with specialized rewards, but leaves low-level artifacts that these rewards may fail to penalize. To address this gap, we propose AdvFidelity, which integrates artifact-sensitive fidelity supervision into RL through an online adversarial reward. This enables joint reward alignment and high-fidelity few-step generation within a single RL stage, without distribution matching distillation (DMD) or other explicit distillation objectives. We train a discriminator to rank high-quality references (positives) above content-matched reconstructions (negatives) produced by the current generator. Reconstructing moderately noised references largely preserves style and scene layout while exposing low-level degradations. This encourages the discriminator to assess artifacts rather than content differences. With negatives reconstructed online, alternating updates adapt fidelity supervision to the generator's evolving failure modes. References can come from existing target-domain data or full-step model samples. Built on LeapAlign, AdvFidelity backpropagates gradients from both rewards through the few-step sampling trajectories used at inference. Across two model backbones and three task settings, AdvFidelity matches full-step LeapAlign in alignment, task performance, and overall generation quality and remains highly competitive with other evaluated full-step RL methods, using only 4 or 8 steps without CFG.

title: 用现成的光学技术,造一台十进制光子连续计算机
abstract: 本文提出利用成熟线偏振光技术构建十进制光子连续计算机的工程方案。通过十个标准偏振方向表示数字,以电场控制旋光直接执行加减运算,利用零点跨圈事件生成进位与借位,并通过十进制补码实现负数及连续累加。系统采用十个等透光率独立阈值卡槽完成数字读取,通过标准光态再发行形成可重复的机器周期,为常温常压下的可编程光学计算提供可实验验证的实现路线。

title: Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories
abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) aims to recover reasoning capabilities in low-bit large language models (LLMs). Existing recipes typically supervise the quantized student with the original full-precision model on fixed response sequences. However, the resulting low-bit quantized models still struggle on long-horizon reasoning tasks and often fail to terminate within a token budget that suffices for the full-precision model. We identify two challenges in closing this gap. First, fixed-response supervision leaves a mismatch between training prefixes and those encountered during student generation, and this trajectory divergence grows as responses lengthen. Second, on its own prefixes, the student underpredicts some next-token candidates and overpredicts others, and this distributional misalignment becomes more frequent at high-entropy prefixes. We present OnQ, a low-bit recovery pipeline that combines on-policy distillation and candidate-wise Dynamic KL. Starting from block-wise calibration, the quantized student generates responses and receives full-precision teacher supervision on its own prefixes. Dynamic KL weights forward and reverse KL by each candidate's teacher-student probability ratio to balance correction of under- and overprediction. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B at 2- and 3-bit precision, OnQ achieves the highest nine-benchmark average, with the largest gains on long-horizon reasoning benchmarks. At 2 bits, it outperforms every baseline on every benchmark at every model size, improving the Qwen3-8B average by 10.26 points over the strongest baseline. It also produces shorter responses with fewer truncations and repetitive errors.

title: Active-Labeling Evaluation for Computer Agriculture Nematode-Cyst Detection Under Sparse Soil-Sample Ground Truth: An Artificial Intelligence Annotation-Efficiency Bound
abstract: Active learning promises to reduce the annotation burden of training nematode-cyst detection models for precision agriculture, but the size of that reduction is not known when ground truth comes from sparse soil samples rather than exhaustive visual inspection. the present analysis derives an annotation-efficiency bound for pool-based active learning under sparse soil-sample ground truth. The detection task is formalised as a two-stage process in which a classifier selects candidate cysts from soil imagery and a laboratory assay confirms a small labelled subset. Under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, the bound is evaluated across a design grid of 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, with 2000 replications per cell. The annotation-efficiency gain is bounded by the ratio of label noise to cluster-level variance, and that 52 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point improvement at 80% power. The bound provides a design rule for allocating annotation effort between active selection and confirmatory soil sampling.

title: A Sharp Dynamic Haussler Lemma
abstract: Haussler's covering lemma (JCTA 1995) gives the sharp $(C/δ)^d$ metric-entropy bound for binary VC classes under normalized $\ell_1$ distance. We prove a sharp global dynamic analogue for bounded real-valued classes in normalized $\ell_p$, for every $1\le p<\infty$. Writing $d=\operatorname{sfat}_{\varepsilon/32}(\mathcal F)$, we obtain a global dynamic cover of size at most $(C/\varepsilon^p)^d$ for every horizon and $0<\varepsilon<1/2$. Here a single family of deterministic causal experts, fixed independently of the instance sequence, covers every target on every sequence. For $0<\varepsilon<1/4$, a matching worst-case lower bound $(c/\varepsilon)^{pd}$ holds already for binary classes on one fixed sequence, even with real-valued experts. The constants are universal, independent of $p$. For $p=2$, this resolves the horizon-independent sequential $\ell_2$ covering problem of Rakhlin, Sridharan, and Tewari (PTRF 2015) in a stronger global form. For $p=1$, it gives the sharp $(C/δ)^{\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal H)}$ global dynamic covering bound for binary classes, resolving questions of Alon, Ben-Eliezer, Dagan, Moran, Naor, and Yogev (STOC 2021) and Malliaris and Moran (Trans. AMS 2024). Our proof combines rank-decreasing correction schedules and accurate sampled prefixes with exact continuations after target identification. Shared-parent routing distributes these continuations among eligible prefixes, eliminating the logarithmic overhead.

title: AOV-GS: Active Open-Vocabulary Semantic Mapping with 3D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Robots deployed in human-centered environments need maps that support both geometric navigation and open-vocabulary semantic queries beyond a fixed label set. A key challenge is enriching such maps with semantic information without relying on manually annotated segmentation masks or closed-set semantic categories. Existing geometry-driven active mapping maximizes coverage but treats semantics as a passive by-product of the collected trajectory, whereas active semantic mapping typically depends on supervised semantic segmentation. We present AOV-GS, an active 3D Gaussian mapping system that guides exploration using frozen foundation models. During coarse exploration, AOV-GS re-ranks geometrically promising candidate views according to CLIP mask-embedding novelty computed from SAM instance segmentation, biasing exploration toward semantically informative regions. Frozen SAM and CLIP provide instance masks and language-aligned embeddings throughout mapping, while a lightweight scene-specific language field is fitted offline directly to the collected CLIP embeddings rather than manually annotated masks, enabling open-vocabulary text-query segmentation on novel views. In a controlled comparison using the same SAM-CLIP perception stack, AOV-GS improves average language-field mIoU over geometry-only active planning by 1.3 percentage points on Replica (34.6% on eight scenes) and by 1.8 points on Matterport3D (23.1% on five scenes). With CorrCLIP, AOV-GS reaches 35.6% on Replica, 2.0 points above the matched Geometry-based + CorrCLIP baseline. Novel-view PSNR remains comparable to the geometry-only baseline on both datasets while depth L1 improves on Replica. Code is available at https://github.com/OptimusFaber/AOV-GS.

title: Interpretability of Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation for Computer-Aided Malaria Parasite Detection Under Giemsa Stain Batch Variation: A Healthcare Robustness Evaluation
abstract: Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) is widely used to attribute the decisions of convolutional networks that screen Giemsa-stained blood films for malaria parasites, yet the stability of those attributions under routine stain-batch variation has not been characterised. the present analysis treats LRP attribution maps as estimators and asks how their agreement degrades when the input distribution shifts along the stain axis. We formalise attribution stability as a variance decomposition in which the between-batch component is the quantity of clinical interest, and we derive a propagation bound showing that the batch-induced perturbation of a relevance map is controlled by the product of the layer-wise gain of the network and the stain-induced input displacement. The bound implies that attribution instability is not a property of LRP alone but of the pairing between a network's local Lipschitz behaviour and the colour statistics of the staining protocol. We then specify a before-after-control-impact design for evaluating attribution stability across stain batches, with a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), and report the operating characteristics of that design across 2000 replications per cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Fifty-four clusters are required for 80% power at a 5-percentage-point effect. The contribution is a formal account of why LRP maps drift under stain variation and a design that makes that drift measurable before deployment.
